messages.subject: (anonymized) fixnode analyses and lnL decreases
parts:
Hi XXX!

A few thoughts...

XXX wrote:
> Hi Nick,
> thanks again for your suggestions. Everything worked perfect now, and I included you in the
> acknowledgments of the manuscript for your technical advices. One last question maybe regarding the
> fixnode analysis. The best-fit model has a worse LnL (-109.9) compared to the best-fit model of the
> unconstrained (-101.5) analysis (in both cases, DEC+J). I think this may be related to degrees of
> freedom, right?



I think of degrees of freedom as basically:

(degrees of freedom) = (number of data) - (number of free parameters estimated from the data)

...so it's not quite that.  Both the fixnode and non-fixnode analyses have the same number of free
parameters and the same tip data.

Really what is going on is this: a fixnode constraint will always lower the lnL, because, at that
node, you are taking:

the original likelihoods-of-the-data-above-the-node, e.g. A=0.1, B=0.15, AB=0.05

...and multiplying by the fixnode constraint:

(A=0.1, B=0.15, AB=0.05) x (0 1 0) --> (A=0, B=0.15, AB=0)

You've zeroed out some of the data likelihood, i.e. ruling out some of the scenarios that could have
explained the tip data.  Therefore the likelihood must go down.


Despite the decrease in likelihood, doing a fixnode analysis might be justifiable for various reasons:

* as adding more data -- fixing the states at a certain node is rather like adding another tip to a
tree, ie adding more data. Adding more data will always lower the likelihood as well (it's another
pattern that the model has to fit, and thus requires more events, each event has a probability cost)

* as reflecting a strong prior -- we aren't officially considering priors in a Maximum Likelihood
analysis, but it is reasonable to impose constraints on ancestor(s) range(s) if there is good evidence
justifying the prior

* as reflecting a hypothesis, e.g. you want to see how other ancestral ranges or parameter estimates
change, if you hypothesize that node-X-for-sure-had-range-B.






 

> In case that some reviewer is asking, why we prefer the fossil-constrained analysis which has a lower
> LnL is there anything to test between these two analyses such as with the +w models for the dispersal
> matrix (as in the Solanaceae paper by Dupin et al.) or is it just comparing apple with oranges and
> these two analyses should not be statistically compared at all?


They could be statistically compared (with AICc, not with LRT), but the comparison will show that the
more-constrained-fixnode-analysis has lower lnL!  But, it might be interesting to ask if the decrease
in model fit is substantial (roughly 2+ units of AICc) or not -- e.g., if the difference is low, then
this is evidence that the unconstrained analysis and the constrained analysis are roughly equally good
fits to the tip data.

 
> I think the latter is true and I would just compare differences in estimated ancestral areas, which
> are anyways only minor.



That is reasonable -- as with most variant analyses, it's all reasonable as long as you explain what
was done and why (or, that should be reasonable enough for reviewers...of course sometimes reviewers
disagree about what is reasonable)

Cheers!
Nick
